answer:
There are **3** possible paths.

Since the first and last impressions are \(L\), the eight positions are

\[
L,\ \_,\ \_,\ \_,\ \_,\ \_,\ \_,\ L
\]

and with exactly four \(L\)'s total, the six middle positions must contain exactly **four \(R\)'s and two \(L\)'s**.

To have exactly one adjacent \(RR\) pair, the four \(R\)'s must form runs of sizes

\[
2,\ 1,\ 1.
\]

The run of two \(R\)'s can be in any one of the three gaps created by the two middle \(L\)'s. Thus the paths are:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&LRRLRLRL,\\
&LRLRRLRL,\\
&LRLRLRRL.
\end{aligned}
\]

For an \(RRR\) run counted by starting position, it contains **two** consecutive-\(R\) pairs:

\[
(R_1,R_2),\quad (R_2,R_3),
\]

because the starting positions are the first and second \(R\) of the run, respectively. In general, a run of \(k\) consecutive \(R\)'s contributes \(k-1\) adjacent \(RR\) pairs when counted by starting position. So an \(RRR\) run would already contribute 2 pairs, exceeding the allowed exactly-one pair.

\[
\boxed{3}
\]
